t: Find a Good Subset of the Matrix — Only Singles and Pairs Matter
o: Each row is a binary string of length n ≤ 5, i.e., a bitmask below 32. A subset of size 1 is good iff the row is all zeros (column sums ≤ floor(1/2)=0). A subset of size 2 is good iff the two rows share no 1 in any column (bitwise AND is 0). A crucial fact: if any good subset exists, one of size 1 or 2 exists — so we never need to search larger subsets. Example 3's two identical rows of all ones fail both tests, hence [].
k: Rows are 5-bit masks; a good pair is simply two masks with AND == 0.

a.i: Convert each row to a mask. If any mask is 0, return that row. Otherwise try all pairs of rows; if two masks AND to 0, return them sorted. Otherwise return [].
s: Map each row to an integer bitmask.
Double-loop over rows; return the first pair with (masks[i] & masks[j]) == 0.
a.t: O(m·n + m²) — building masks plus the pairwise scan (at most 31 distinct nonzero masks matter)

w: The key lemma to state in an interview: any good subset can be shrunk to a good subset of size ≤ 2 (repeatedly drop a row whose removal keeps column sums within floor(k/2); a minimally good subset has size 1 or 2). Pitfall: remember the size-1 case requires an entirely zero row.
